hint: This is one function divided by another, so the quotient rule applies. Remember that the order of the two terms on top matters.

hints.text: This is one function divided by another, so the quotient rule applies. Remember that the order of the two terms on top matters.

Use $\frac{u'v - uv'}{v^2}$ with top $u = 2x + 1$ (derivative $2$) and bottom $v = x - 3$ (derivative $1$). That gives $g'(x) = \frac{2(x - 3) - (2x + 1)(1)}{(x - 3)^2}$. Simplify the top, then substitute $x = 4$.
The top simplifies to $-7$, so $g'(x) = \frac{-7}{(x - 3)^2}$ and $g'(4) = \frac{-7}{1} = -7$.

explanation: The top of the quotient rule is $u'v - uv' = 2(x - 3) - (2x + 1) = 2x - 6 - 2x - 1 = -7$.
The bottom of the quotient rule is the old denominator squared, so $g'(x) = \frac{-7}{(x - 3)^2}$.
At $x = 4$ this is $\frac{-7}{(1)^2} = -7$. The graph is falling steeply just right of its asymptote at $x = 3$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Rewrite, then differentiate
steps: The constant $2$ has derivative $0$, and $\frac{7}{x - 3} = 7(x - 3)^{-1}$ has derivative $-7(x - 3)^{-2}$.
At $x = 4$: $-7 \cdot 1 = -7$. Same answer, no quotient rule needed.
